Drive this operation from the by-hand commands in APPLY rather than from the helper's apply mode. iam:ADDS ssm:GetParameter on the fence-lease parameter to the control-plane API role. In the synthesized closure this grant lands in the role's OVERFLOW managed policy, not its default policy, and the overflow split also relocates the pre-existing ec2:DescribeLaunchTemplateVersions statement from overflow policy 1 to overflow policy 2 — a repackaging with no change in effective permissions. So both overflow policies show as modified while exactly one permission is new. On a live deployment the operator adds a small inline policy instead of reproducing the split, and must not remove ec2:DescribeLaunchTemplateVersions from wherever it currently sits. If this deployment also runs a lifecycle-consumer function, the same grant belongs on ITS role too: the consumer is the primary executor of async lifecycle actions, and the reference configuration used for this closure has the queue path off, so no consumer resource appears here.

operations.resource: lambda:SETS two dispatch knobs as environment variables on BOTH openclaw-api and openclaw-lifecycle-consumer, lowering the ssm:SendCommand call rate. Neither knob is injected by the stack in this range, so the effective value is the code default in core/clients.py (6 and 0.5) and those two lines already honour an env override, so no code changes. The live map is read back and MERGED, never replaced: update-function-configuration takes a COMPLETE Variables map, so passing only these two keys deletes every other variable the function holds, and this op refuses to write when the readback is empty. Both functions must change or the two sides run different values. It owns no synthesized resource ref because the knobs are an operational parameter change rather than part of this diff range, and it needs review for exactly that reason.

fixes.summary: The lifecycle fence lease stops being a frozen Lambda env value and becomes SSM parameter /openclaw/lifecycle/fence-lease-sec (default 240s, hard floor 210s = the delete action's exec_sec budget), read per call with a 60s in-process cache. Before this, LIFECYCLE_FENCE_LEASE_SECONDS was baked at 1800s into a published Lambda version, so editing it had no effect on live traffic at all.
fixes.applies_when: always for this kit: the api and lifecycle-consumer functions both read the new parameter, and both roles need ssm:GetParameter on it

params_changed.name: lifecycle fence lease seconds (SSM parameter /openclaw/lifecycle/fence-lease-sec)
params_changed.old_default: 1800 (env LIFECYCLE_FENCE_LEASE_SECONDS, frozen on the published version)
params_changed.runtime_impact: A tenant whose lifecycle operation dies mid-flight is now re-takeable after 240s instead of 1800s, so a crashed worker no longer parks the tenant for half an hour. The floor exists because a lease shorter than a real operation gets that operation killed by its own host_guard (exit 79): for restart that leaves the VM stopped while status still reads running, and for delete the guard fires after delete-vm.sh so the VM and data disk are already gone. Raising the value is safe; lowering it below 210 is refused at synth and at runtime. Future hosts are unaffected (no LT or userdata change). Steady-state SSM read cost is about 0.8 TPS against a 40 TPS shared quota.

fixes.summary: client_token now derives a stable operation id for restart and delete, so re-entering with the same token reports progress as 202 with retry_after_sec instead of dispatching the destructive command a second time. A genuine conflict answers 409 carrying retry_after_sec, and acquire(allow_reentry=False) closes the non-atomic check-then-act window where two concurrent requests sharing one client_token could both obtain the same valid epoch and both dispatch.

A new suspend_failed state is split by whether a usable backup exists, so an operator can tell 'retry the suspend' from 'the data is safe, retry the restore'. delete from suspend_failed takes a no-ledger path (the host is gone, there is nothing to detach and the token was already returned), and the half that holds suspend_backup_key is allowed to restore.

restore has no failed terminal state. A pre-launch brake stops a doomed restore before it boots a VM, the deadline executor demotes the in-flight suspend/restore case to a recorder instead of flipping status to failed, and the reaper carries a restore compensation tier that releases a stuck reservation.

params_changed.name: ENFORCED_QUIET_SEC (health_check env, code default)
params_changed.old_default: did not exist before this patch
params_changed.runtime_impact: How long a fence-enforced tenant must stay quiet before the reaper settles it. Too low re-settles a tenant whose command is still in flight; the kit ships the code default and adds no Lambda env, so the effective value is 150s unless the operator sets the env deliberately.

params_changed.name: ENFORCED_MAX_PER_SWEEP (health_check env, code default)
params_changed.old_default: did not exist before this patch
params_changed.runtime_impact: Caps how many enforced tenants one reaper sweep settles, bounding the blast radius of a wrong verdict to two tenants per sweep. Raising it speeds convergence and widens that radius.

fixes.summary: Host death is confirmed against EC2 rather than inferred from a missing or deleted hosts-table row, because a row can be wrongly deleted while the machine is still alive — writing suspend_failed on that clue alone would mark a tenant with a live VM as terminal. The host termination cleaner now yields to a tenant that can still be recovered instead of reclaiming it, and a failed evacuation backup no longer counts as 'safe to reclaim'.

POST /hosts/egress/allow/validate reports each unavailable protected-network criterion on its own line instead of one warning that only fired when every coordinate was missing. In an environment that derives TENANT_SUPERNET from VM_SUBNET_PREFIX but has no VPC_CIDR, the old warning could never appear, while 'the check that stops a hole covering the whole VPC is not running here' is exactly what the operator needs to know.

The pre-launch validator ships as a first-class operator tool: it checks all 11 data-plane delivery channels plus control-plane drift and reports PASS / FAIL / NOT JUDGED per channel rather than one aggregate verdict. It reads live state only; it never writes. PR #229 added the channel and control-plane coverage and PR #234 dropped two unused imports and pointed the kits at this path.
fixes.applies_when: OPTIONAL — the operator decides. The 19 files are staged under lib/validator/ and run on the operator host with read-only credentials; they are not deployed to AWS and no other fix in this kit depends on them. Skipping the tool leaves every other fix fully applied.

fixes.summary: Lower the ssm:SendCommand call rate on the create path: SPREAD_MAX_HOSTS_PER_BATCH 6 -> 3 and HOST_SELECTION_SCORE_FLOOR 0.5 -> 0.25, as environment variables on both openclaw-api and openclaw-lifecycle-consumer. One SendCommand goes out per host in a batch, so capping the spread at 3 hosts halves the calls per batch while each call carries proportionally more tenants. The score floor narrows the weighted-random spread so placement concentrates, which is what keeps a batch inside the lower host cap.
fixes.applies_when: when this deployment is hitting ssm:SendCommand throttling on create bursts. This is an operational tuning step, independent of the code in this range: applying it needs no other fix here, and skipping it leaves every other fix intact.

params_changed.name: SPREAD_MAX_HOSTS_PER_BATCH (Lambda env on both functions)
params_changed.old_default: 6 (code default in core/clients.py; not injected by the stack in this range)
params_changed.runtime_impact: Halves the SendCommand calls a create batch issues, because there is one call per host. The same tenants land on fewer hosts, so each host takes proportionally more of them. Known cost: placement concentrates, so one host's cold-start queue gets longer — the host-side launch-slot flock means the tail VMs of a batch start later, and a tail approaching the SSM executionTimeout risks the 'false tail timeout rolls back a live VM' shape. Judge a batch by the MAX end-to-end time to running, not the mean. Future hosts are unaffected: no Launch Template or userdata change.

params_changed.name: HOST_SELECTION_SCORE_FLOOR (Lambda env on both functions)
params_changed.old_default: 0.5 (code default in core/clients.py; not injected by the stack in this range)
params_changed.runtime_impact: Lower floor on the weighted-random host score, so a low-scoring host is less likely to be chosen and placement concentrates further. It does not itself change the number of commands; it is what keeps a batch inside the narrower host cap above, and it carries the same concentration cost.

verifications.pass_when: an integer >= 210 is returned (240 unless the operator raised it)
verifications.fail_when: ParameterNotFound (the AUTO_CLI put-parameter step was skipped) or a value below 210 (a hand-edit below the floor; fence_config rejects it at runtime and falls back to 240, so the operator's intent silently does not apply)

verifications.action: aws iam simulate-principal-policy --policy-source-arn <api role arn> --action-names ssm:GetParameter --resource-arns arn:aws:ssm:$AWS_REGION:$ACCOUNT:parameter/openclaw/lifecycle/fence-lease-sec ; repeat for the lifecycle-consumer role
verifications.pass_when: allowed for BOTH the api role and the lifecycle-consumer role
verifications.fail_when: implicitDeny on either role. The consumer is the primary executor of async lifecycle actions, so a missing grant there produces the worst shape: api reads the parameter while consumer silently falls back to the code default, and the two diverge the moment an operator edits the value. Note the IAM data plane can lag the simulator by minutes — re-run rather than trusting a single result.

verifications.action: Two-sided, and NOT from an application log line — the code has none on the success path. (a) CloudTrail: look up ssm:GetParameter events whose requestParameters.name is /openclaw/lifecycle/fence-lease-sec over the last hour and group them by the calling role. (b) The api and lifecycle-consumer log groups: search for the fence_config fallback lines, which are the ONLY thing that module prints and which appear only when the SSM read failed.
verifications.observable: the per-role GetParameter count on that parameter, and the presence or absence of a fence_config fallback log line
verifications.pass_when: BOTH roles show at least one GetParameter on that parameter, AND neither log group contains a fence_config fallback line. Combined with V1 (the parameter reads an integer >= 210) that establishes the effective lease.
verifications.fail_when: Only the api role appears and the consumer role does not — that is exactly the divergence shape where api honours the parameter while the consumer silently uses its code default, and it means the consumer is not running the patched fence_config. Or a fallback line is present: the read failed, so the effective value came from a stale cache or the default and may coincidentally equal 240 while nothing is actually reading SSM. Do NOT judge this from a source= log line: fence_config prints nothing on success, and _lease_seconds discards the source it receives. Do NOT judge it from the tenant row's active_lifecycle_until either: the production consumer renews that field while you read it. /system/info reports the deadline snapshot, which is a different mechanism.
verifications.cleanup: none — CloudTrail and log search are read-only

verifications.action: Send DELETE /tenants/{id} twice with the identical client_token, the second call while the first is still in flight; capture both HTTP statuses and bodies, then count the SSM SendCommand invocations for that tenant in CloudTrail.
verifications.observable: the two HTTP responses and the SendCommand count
verifications.pass_when: both calls answer 202, the second body carries retry_after_sec, and exactly ONE SendCommand was issued for the tenant
verifications.fail_when: two SendCommand invocations (re-entry dispatched a second destructive command and the two can interleave around the unlocked sleep 2 window), or the second call answers 409 (the stable-op-id derivation from client_token is not active)
verifications.cleanup: the tenant is deleted by the action under test; confirm it reached deleted

verifications.action: While one lifecycle action holds the lease, send a DIFFERENT action for the same tenant with a different client_token and read the error body.
verifications.pass_when: HTTP 409 whose body contains an integer retry_after_sec > 0
verifications.fail_when: 409 without retry_after_sec (pre-patch bytes), or 202 (the fence is not holding at all, which is a far worse finding than a missing field)
verifications.cleanup: let the in-flight action finish, then delete the tenant

verifications.action: Drive a tenant into suspend_failed by terminating its host mid-suspend, then read the tenant row and attempt the exit the row advertises: restore when suspend_backup_key is present, delete when it is not.
verifications.observable: tenant status, suspend_backup_key presence, and the exit's outcome
verifications.pass_when: status is suspend_failed, and the advertised exit succeeds: restore returns the tenant to running with its data disk intact, or delete reaches deleted without touching the capacity ledger a second time
verifications.fail_when: the tenant has no exit (both restore and delete refuse), or delete double-debits the ledger, or restore is offered while suspend_backup_key is absent
verifications.cleanup: delete the tenant by its exact id; confirm the real-tenant count is unchanged

verifications.action: Force a restore past its deadline (a host that cannot serve it), then watch the tenant row and the reaper log across at least two sweeps.
verifications.observable: tenant status transitions and the reaper's compensation decision
verifications.pass_when: the tenant never lands on a restore_failed terminal state, the pre-launch brake stops it before a VM boots, and the reaper releases the stuck reservation
verifications.fail_when: a VM boots for a doomed restore, or the reservation stays held after two sweeps, or status flips to failed. Watch for longer than one sweep interval — a window shorter than the retry cadence proves nothing.
verifications.cleanup: delete the tenant by its exact id

verifications.action: aws iam simulate-principal-policy --policy-source-arn <health role arn> --action-names ec2:DescribeInstances --resource-arns '*'
verifications.fail_when: implicitDeny — _host_is_dead cannot reach EC2, so the reaper falls back to the hosts-table clue and can write suspend_failed for a tenant whose VM is still running

verifications.action: POST /hosts/egress/allow/validate with a /16 destination, in an environment whose api function has no VPC_CIDR/EGRESS_VPC_CIDR env, and read warnings[]
verifications.pass_when: a warning naming VPC_CIDR/EGRESS_VPC_CIDR appears on its own, independent of whether TENANT_SUPERNET is configured
verifications.fail_when: the single combined 'neither VPC_CIDR ... nor TENANT_SUPERNET' wording appears, or warnings is empty — pre-patch bytes, where the warning could not fire in an environment that derives TENANT_SUPERNET
verifications.cleanup: none — validate is a dry run and writes nothing

verifications.action: OPTIONAL, and last — run it only if you want an independent pre-launch sweep. Nothing in this kit depends on it. Offline first: python3 -m pytest lib/validator/test -q  (no AWS access needed). Then, if you choose to point it at the environment: lib/validator/oc-prelaunch-validate with read-only credentials.
verifications.observable: the pytest summary and the per-channel verdict table
verifications.pass_when: If you run it: pytest reports a non-zero passed count with zero failures, and the tool prints a verdict for each of the 11 delivery channels plus the control-plane drift check. Declining to run it is a valid outcome and does not block this kit.
verifications.fail_when: zero tests collected or every test skipped (a green exit that proves nothing), or a channel silently absent from the table rather than reported NOT JUDGED

verifications.action: lib/apply-resource-ops.sh lambda-env-spread-and-floor verify — reads the consumer's env first, then reads the env of the VERSION the api function's live alias actually serves.
verifications.observable: the two variables on each side, read from the version that serves traffic
verifications.pass_when: both functions report SPREAD_MAX_HOSTS_PER_BATCH=3 and HOST_SELECTION_SCORE_FLOOR=0.25
verifications.fail_when: the api side reports None or the old value while the consumer reports 3 and 0.25. That is the frozen-environment trap rather than a missed command: the api serves traffic through a published version whose environment is a snapshot, and update-function-configuration writes only $LATEST. Either publish a version and move the alias, or accept that the knobs are consumer-side only — and state which. Also fail if any OTHER variable disappeared from either function, which means a whole-map replacement happened instead of a merge.

verifications.action: Run one create burst the same size as a pre-change baseline run, then count ssm:SendCommand events for it in CloudTrail and record the MAX end-to-end time to running.
verifications.observable: SendCommand count per batch, and the slowest tenant's time to running
verifications.pass_when: the per-batch SendCommand count drops to at most 3 from 6, and every tenant still reaches running
verifications.fail_when: any tenant stalls in creating past the boot window, or the slowest tenant's time to running crosses the SSM executionTimeout — that is the concentration cost landing, and it is why the judgement is the max rather than the mean. Note SendCommand throttling is visible only in CloudTrail; scanning application logs for it returns zero, and that zero is not evidence.
verifications.cleanup: delete the burst tenants by their exact recorded ids, never a prefix glob
